result.markdown: --- course-unit: ch12-data-to-decision-capstone status: complete --- # Data-to-decision capstone This capstone follows one analysis from a committed data file to a conditional intervention comparison. The point is not to make a historical claim from a small table. It is to make every transition visible: provenance, model choice, fitting, diagnostics, uncertainty, sensitivity, and a decision-relevant scenario. ## Learning goals By the end of this chapter you should be able to: - load and verify a versioned local dataset without a render-time download; - distinguish observations from reconstructed latent SIR states; - fit a small ODE model with bounded `Optimization.jl` parameters; - diagnose fit mismatch and summarize deterministic parameter uncertainty; - propagate parameter changes through a sensitivity calculation; and - compare an intervention scenario with its no-intervention counterfactual. ## Model assumptions and classification The data are the eight committed Eyam observations described in [`data/README.md`](../data/README.md) and `data/eyam_plague_1666.toml`. They cover the second wave beginning on 18 June 1666, with a modeled population of 261. The historical context is discussed by Raggett (@raggett1982) and by the later epidemiological analysis of Whittles and Didelot (@whittles2016). We choose a deterministic, continuous-time, continuous-state, homogeneous closed SIR model because it is the smallest model that connects the three columns and the preceding course units. This is a deliberately limited model choice. The `S` and `I` values are **reconstructed from historical records and model assumptions, not direct measurements**. A homogeneous closed SIR model also omits important plague mechanisms, including rodent-to-human transmission, household structure, population movement, and changing reporting. The modeled population is the population at the start of the second wave, not the pre-plague village population. ## Equations For this small dataset we fit an effective transmission rate $\lambda=\beta c$ and a recovery/removal rate $\gamma$: $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm dS}{\mathrm dt} &= -\lambda\frac{SI}{N},\\ \frac{\mathrm dI}{\mathrm dt} &= \lambda\frac{SI}{N}-\gamma I,\\ \frac{\mathrm dR}{\mathrm dt} &= \gamma I. \end{aligned} $$ {#eq-capstone-sir} The initial state is fixed to the first row, and the fitted trajectory is compared with all three reconstructed state columns. For an intervention scenario we add cumulative incidence $C$ and multiply $\lambda$ by $1-v(t)$: $$ \frac{\mathrm dC}{\mathrm dt} = (1-v(t))\lambda\frac{SI}{N}. $$ {#eq-capstone-intervention} The least-squares objective is $$ L(\lambda,\gamma)= \sum_{k=1}^{8}\sum_{j\in\{S,I,R\}} \left(\frac{x_j(t_k;\lambda,\gamma)-x_{j,k}}{N}\right)^2. $$ {#eq-capstone-loss} This is a transparent teaching objective, not a claim that historical counts have Gaussian errors. A count likelihood, reporting model, or mechanistic plague model would be appropriate for a substantive historical analysis. ## Julia implementation The data path is local and the fallback is deterministic. The checksum is checked only for the committed file; no code in this chapter fetches epidemiological data from the network. ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using CairoMakie using CSV using DataFrames using DiffEqCallbacks using OrdinaryDiffEq using Optimization using OptimizationOptimJL using SHA using TOML course_root = normpath(joinpath(@__DIR__, "..")) include(joinpath(course_root, "src", "EpiModelingCourse.jl")) using .EpiModelingCourse data_path = joinpath(course_root, "data", "eyam_plague_1666.csv") metadata_path = joinpath(course_root, "data", "eyam_plague_1666.toml") metadata = TOML.parsefile(metadata_path) population = Float64(metadata["population"]) observation_columns = [:time_months, :S, :I, :R] function deterministic_fallback(N) times = [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 4.0] initial = [N - 7.0, 7.0, 0.0] fallback_rhs!(du, u, p, t) = begin λ, γ = p S, I, R = u incidence = λ * S * I / N du[1] = -incidence du[2] = incidence - γ * I du[3] = γ * I nothing end solution = solve( ODEProblem(fallback_rhs!, initial, (first(times), last(times)), [1.0, 0.5]), Tsit5(); saveat = times, abstol = 1e-9, reltol = 1e-9, ) states = Array(solution) return DataFrame( time_months = times, S = states[1, :], I = states[2, :], R = states[3, :], ) end data_is_committed = isfile(data_path) data = data_is_committed ? CSV.read(data_path, DataFrame) : deterministic_fallback(population) data_source = data_is_committed ? "committed Eyam CSV" : "deterministic synthetic fallback" if data_is_committed actual_checksum = bytes2hex(sha256(read(data_path))) @assert actual_checksum == metadata["csv_sha256"] end @assert String.(names(data)) == String.(observation_columns) @assert nrow(data) == 8 @assert all(diff(data.time_months) .> 0) @assert all(isapprox.(data.S .+ data.I .+ data.R, population; atol = 1e-8)) ``` ::: The metadata records the expected SHA-256 digest, the packaged MultiBD source, and the Apache 2.0 license. A checksum verifies that this checkout contains the committed bytes; it does not prove that the historical reconstruction is correct. Provenance and interpretation caveats remain part of the model decision. ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} data_source, metadata["provenance"], metadata["interpretation"]["caveats"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ("committed Eyam CSV", Dict{String, Any}("primary_record" => "Burial register of St. Lawrence Church, Eyam, Derbyshire", "analytical_source" => "Raggett, G. F. (1982), A stochastic model of the Eyam plague", "packaged_source_url" => "https://github.com/msuchard/MultiBD", "analytical_source_doi" => "10.1080/02664768200000021", "packaged_source_file" => "R/Eyam.R and data/Eyam.rda", "packaged_source_file_sha" => "1f0947c3777216360e8eeb16c774ebe7109a9b57", "packaged_source" => "MultiBD 1.0.2", "packaged_source_license" => "Apache License 2.0"), ["The population of 261 is the population at the start of the second wave, not the pre-plague village population.", "The S and I series are model-derived reconstructions from historical records rather than direct measurements.", "A simple closed homogeneous SIR model omits possible rodent-to-human transmission and population movement.", "The final observation is one month after the preceding observation; earlier intervals are half a month."]) ``` ::: ::: ### Fitting the effective SIR model The fitting kernel is deliberately visible. Its `λ` parameter is an effective rate; it should not be reported as a separately identified contact rate and transmission probability. ::: {#6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} observation_times = Float64.(data.time_months) initial_state = Float64.(collect(data[1, [:S, :I, :R]])) observed_states = permutedims(Matrix{Float64}(data[:, [:S, :I, :R]])) function fit_rhs!(du, u, p, t) λ, γ = p S, I, R = u incidence = λ * S * I / population du[1] = -incidence du[2] = incidence - γ * I du[3] = γ * I return nothing end function fit_loss(θ, _) problem = ODEProblem( fit_rhs!, initial_state, (first(observation_times), last(observation_times)), θ, ) solution = solve( problem, Tsit5(); saveat = observation_times, abstol = 1e-8, reltol = 1e-8, ) prediction = Array(solution) return sum(((prediction .- observed_states) ./ population) .^ 2) end coarse_grid = [ (fit_loss([λ, γ], nothing), λ, γ) for λ in range(0.5, 6.0; length = 15) for γ in range(0.5, 4.0; length = 15) ] grid_start = coarse_grid[argmin(first.(coarse_grid))] fit_objective = OptimizationFunction(fit_loss, AutoFiniteDiff()) fit_problem = OptimizationProblem( fit_objective, [grid_start[2], grid_start[3]], nothing; lb = [1e-4, 1e-4], ub = [8.0, 8.0], ) fit_solution = solve(fit_problem, Fminbox(LBFGS()); maxiters = 60) fitted_parameters = Float64.(fit_solution.u) fitted_loss = fit_solution.objective fitted_parameters, fitted_loss ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ([4.603717504388643, 2.8076873724509857], 0.00390067987740599) ``` ::: ::: ### Diagnostics The model and data are shown together, followed by residuals. The residual pattern is more useful than a single loss value: systematic timing or peak mismatch is evidence that the homogeneous SIR mechanism is inadequate for the question. ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fitted_solution = solve( ODEProblem( fit_rhs!, initial_state, (first(observation_times), last(observation_times)), fitted_parameters, ), Tsit5(); saveat = observation_times, abstol = 1e-8, reltol = 1e-8, ) fitted_states = Array(fitted_solution) residuals = fitted_states .- observed_states state_rmse = sqrt.(vec(sum(residuals .^ 2; dims = 2)) ./ nrow(data)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3-element Vector{Float64}: 3.670787952976688 2.9810634731108814 3.294442762389717 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-ch12-fit-diagnostics .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fig = Figure(size = (950, 750)) ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "months since 18 June 1666", ylabel = "people") state_labels = ["S", "I", "R"] state_colors = [:steelblue, :firebrick, :seagreen] for j in 1:3 lines!(ax1, observation_times, fitted_states[j, :], color = state_colors[j], label = "$(state_labels[j]) model") scatter!(ax1, observation_times, observed_states[j, :], color = state_colors[j], markersize = 9, label = "$(state_labels[j]) data") end axislegend(ax1, position = :rb, nbanks = 2) ax2 = Axis(fig[2, 1], xlabel = "months since 18 June 1666", ylabel = "model − data") for j in 1:3 lines!(ax2, observation_times, residuals[j, :], color = state_colors[j], label = state_labels[j]) end hlines!(ax2, [0.0], color = :black, linestyle = :dash) axislegend(ax2) fig ``` ::: {#fig-ch12-fit-diagnostics .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Fitted homogeneous SIR states and residuals for the committed Eyam observations. ::: ::: ### Deterministic uncertainty envelope The historical states are reconstructed and there are only eight rows, so a formal confidence interval would require an explicit observation model. As a transparent alternative, we construct a deterministic parameter envelope: the $3\times3$ combinations of $\pm10\%$ around the fitted parameters are retained when their loss is close to the best loss. This is an uncertainty scenario, not a calibrated confidence interval. ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} parameter_candidates = [ fitted_parameters .* [λ_scale, γ_scale] for λ_scale in [0.9, 1.0, 1.1] for γ_scale in [0.9, 1.0, 1.1] ] accepted_parameters = [ parameters for parameters in parameter_candidates if fit_loss(parameters, nothing) <= fitted_loss + 0.02 ] accepted_predictions = [ Array(solve( ODEProblem( fit_rhs!, initial_state, (first(observation_times), last(observation_times)), parameters, ), Tsit5(); saveat = observation_times, )) for parameters in accepted_parameters ] infectious_lower = [minimum(prediction[2, k] for prediction in accepted_predictions) for k in eachindex(observation_times)] infectious_upper = [maximum(prediction[2, k] for prediction in accepted_predictions) for k in eachindex(observation_times)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 8-element Vector{Float64}: 7.0 15.727944224022478 25.33432858497662 27.360744384133206 25.226216734403867 18.844113632828964 12.29208288038851 4.273587559998206 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-ch12-uncertainty .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fig = Figure(size = (850, 450)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "months since 18 June 1666", ylabel = "infectious people") band!(ax, observation_times, infectious_lower, infectious_upper, color = (:steelblue, 0.25), label = "±10% parameter envelope") lines!(ax, observation_times, fitted_states[2, :], color = :firebrick, label = "fitted model") scatter!(ax, observation_times, observed_states[2, :], color = :black, label = "reconstructed I") axislegend(ax) fig ``` ::: {#fig-ch12-uncertainty .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` A deterministic local parameter envelope for infectious prevalence. ::: ::: ### Sensitivity and intervention comparison For a decision-oriented output, we propagate the fitted parameters to the final cumulative incidence. The centered one-percent perturbation is a local sensitivity check; it is not a replacement for the broader analysis in Chapter 10. ::: {#16 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function decision_rhs!(du, u, p, t) λ, γ, reduction, N = p S, I, R, C = u incidence = (1 - reduction) * λ * S * I / N du[1] = -incidence du[2] = incidence - γ * I du[3] = γ * I du[4] = incidence return nothing end function decision_solution( start_time; duration = 1.0, reduction = 0.5, horizon = 8.0, ) stop_time = start_time + duration parameters = [fitted_parameters[1], fitted_parameters[2], 0.0, population] problem = ODEProblem( decision_rhs!, [initial_state..., 0.0], (0.0, horizon), parameters, ) if duration <= 0.0 || reduction <= 0.0 return solve(problem, Tsit5(); saveat = 0.1) end function affect!(integrator) integrator.p[3] = integrator.t < stop_time ? reduction : 0.0 return nothing end callback = PresetTimeCallback([start_time, stop_time], affect!) return solve(problem, Tsit5(); callback = callback, saveat = 0.1) end function final_cumulative(start_time; duration = 1.0, reduction = 0.5) return Array(decision_solution( start_time; duration = duration, reduction = reduction, ))[4, end] end function final_cumulative_for_parameters(parameters) solution = solve( ODEProblem( decision_rhs!, [initial_state..., 0.0], (0.0, 8.0), [parameters[1], parameters[2], 0.0, population], ), Tsit5(); saveat = 0.1, ) return Array(solution)[4, end] end function relative_parameter_sensitivity(parameter_index) perturbation = 0.01 * fitted_parameters[parameter_index] lower = copy(fitted_parameters) upper = copy(fitted_parameters) lower[parameter_index] -= perturbation upper[parameter_index] += perturbation lower_output = final_cumulative_for_parameters(lower) upper_output = final_cumulative_for_parameters(upper) baseline_output = final_cumulative_for_parameters(fitted_parameters) return (upper_output - lower_output) / (2 * perturbation) * fitted_parameters[parameter_index] / baseline_output end local_loss_sensitivity = [ relative_parameter_sensitivity(index) for index in 1:2 ] no_policy = decision_solution(0.0; duration = 0.0, reduction = 0.0) policy = decision_solution(1.0; duration = 1.0, reduction = 0.5) decision_summary = ( λ = fitted_parameters[1], γ = fitted_parameters[2], final_incidence_without_policy = Array(no_policy)[4, end], final_incidence_with_policy = Array(policy)[4, end], local_loss_sensitivity = local_loss_sensitivity, ) decision_summary ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (λ = 4.603717504388643, γ = 2.8076873724509857, final_incidence_without_policy = 170.942665854259, final_incidence_with_policy = 138.13851031114234, local_loss_sensitivity = [1.1369942301630875, -1.1359021476043987]) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-ch12-decision-comparison .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fig = Figure(size = (900, 500)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "months", ylabel = "cumulative incidence") decision_times = no_policy.t no_policy_array = Array(no_policy) policy_array = Array(policy(decision_times)) lines!(ax, decision_times, no_policy_array[4, :], color = :firebrick, label = "no intervention") lines!(ax, decision_times, policy_array[4, :], color = :steelblue, label = "50% reduction from month 1") vspan!(ax, 1.0, 2.0, color = (:steelblue, 0.15)) axislegend(ax) fig ``` ::: {#fig-ch12-decision-comparison .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Counterfactual cumulative incidence with and without a one-month 50% reduction. ::: ::: ## Validation The data checks validate schema, ordering, population conservation, and the committed checksum. The model checks validate conservation and finite fit output; the decision comparison checks that the chosen intervention lowers cumulative incidence for this fitted scenario. These are structural checks, not evidence that the model is historically adequate. ::: {#20 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fit_conservation_error = maximum( abs.(vec(sum(fitted_states; dims = 1)) .- population), ) fit_is_finite = all(isfinite, fitted_states) policy_reduction = Array(no_policy)[4, end] - Array(policy)[4, end] @assert fit_conservation_error < 1e-6 @assert fit_is_finite @assert policy_reduction > 0 (source = data_source, fit_conservation_error = fit_conservation_error, state_rmse = state_rmse, policy_reduction = policy_reduction) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (source = "committed Eyam CSV", fit_conservation_error = 5.684341886080802e-14, state_rmse = [3.670787952976688, 2.9810634731108814, 3.294442762389717], policy_reduction = 32.80415554311665) ``` ::: ::: ## Interpretation and limitations The fitted $\lambda$ summarizes transmission under the data's time scale; it does not identify separate $\beta$ and $c$. The deterministic envelope captures only a deliberately narrow local perturbation and the residual diagnostic shows why uncertainty should not be reduced to optimizer digits. The intervention comparison is a counterfactual under the same homogeneous closed SIR assumptions. In particular, because `S` and `I` are reconstructed values and a homogeneous closed SIR omits important plague mechanisms, the policy result is an educational model-based comparison, not a historical estimate of the effect of a specific Eyam action. Replacing the model with a household, vector-borne, movement, or observation model would change both the fit and the decision. ## Exercises ### Exercise 1 {#ch12-ex1} Replace the state least-squares loss with a loss on `I` only, refit $(\lambda,\gamma)$, and compare the residual plot and fitted final cumulative incidence with the all-state fit. Explain which information is discarded and why a seemingly better infectious curve may give a worse population balance. ### Exercise 2 {#ch12-ex2} Use the deterministic envelope to compare a one-month 25% reduction with a one-month 50% reduction beginning at month 1. Report the range of final cumulative incidence across accepted parameter candidates for each scenario, then state what additional observation or mechanistic assumption would be needed before treating that range as decision uncertainty. ## Companion materials - [Slides](../slides/chapters/12-data-to-decision-capstone.html) - [Pluto preview](../notebook-exports/chapters/12-data-to-decision-capstone.html) - [Pluto source](../notebooks/chapters/12-data-to-decision-capstone.jl)
